name: Timber Joint Aesthetics: Five Joint Designs
description:
Faithful replication of Kuys & Mridha (2024), "Aesthetic Preference of Timber Joints in Architectural Products", Sustainability 16:154. Participants see a timber pagoda and five designs for the joint between a post and the roof beams, from simple and angular (Joint 1) to ornate and curved (Joint 5). For each joint they rate seven statements on a 7-point agreement scale: looks strong, functional, difficult to manufacture, long-lasting, innovative, appropriate for the overall structure, and overall aesthetically pleasing. Background questions follow the paper's sample description (gender, age, education, ethnicity, employment, occupation). The pictures are the authors' SolidWorks renderings printed as Figure 1 of the open-access paper (CC BY 4.0), used with credit for research; the template is removed if the authors object.

Differences from the original study: (1) the paper names the seven attributes but prints the exact wording only for "Overall, the joint is aesthetically pleasing" and "looks difficult to manufacture"; the other statements are worded "The joint looks …"; (2) the 7-point scale is shown as numbers 1–7 with end and mid labels; (3) the five joints are shown in random order per participant; (4) only the six background questions reported in the paper are asked (the original had nine), using the paper's reported categories.
author: Kuys & Mridha

pages.intro: A timber pagoda is being designed. You will see five ways of joining its posts and roof beams and say how each one looks to you. It takes about 6 minutes and your answers are anonymous.

elements.title: How much do you agree?
elements.description: Joint 1 (paper Figure 1; complexity and curvature rise from Joint 1, angular, to Joint 5, ornate and curved). Seven visual-appearance statements on a 7-point agreement scale (1 strongly disagree … 7 strongly agree). Value: {strong, functional, difficult_to_manufacture, long_lasting, innovative, appropriate, aesthetically_pleasing}. The five joint pages are shown in random order per participant. Analysis in the paper: per-joint agreement and one-way ANOVA of each statement by sociodemographic group (employment was the only significant factor).
